summary: Sauti ya Dunia ("Voice of the Earth" in Swahili) lets anyone hear how their town's climate has changed. Pick a place on a NASA satellite map, ask a question (Is it getting hotter? Is the rain changing? Is the land drying out?) and the app plays the place's 12 months from the past, then today, then both together, as music generated live from NASA measurements. A clash between the two tunes means the climate changed. It ends with a plain-language answer, a then/now chart and, for researchers, a full statistics panel with a 45-year trend test, CSV export and citation. An EIC frame view plays NASA Earth visual frames (night lights, true-colour Earth, sea temperature, vegetation, land heat, or any frame from NASA's Earth Information Center gallery) as sound in real time. Because it works through sound, narration and a screen-reader live region, it also opens NASA Earth data to blind and low-vision people.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Earth information is usually shown as pictures, which leaves out blind and low-vision people and anyone who does not read charts easily. Sauti ya Dunia ("Voice of the Earth" in Swahili) turns NASA Earth data into music you can understand:

1. Choose a country (219 countries, cities load automatically) and a city, or tap anywhere on the NASA GIBS satellite map.

2. Choose a question: HEAT (air temperature), RAIN (rainfall) or GREEN (vegetation greenness), and the years to compare (default 2001–05 vs 2020–24, any range from 1981 to 2025).

3. Press Listen. You hear THEN (12 months, one note each, soft piano), NOW (warm electric piano), then both together over a chord pad. Higher note = warmer / wetter / greener; raindrops = rain; silence = no data. While it plays, NASA's monthly map layer for that month fades in over the place.

4. You get the answer: a big number (e.g. "+86% rain"), one sentence, what it means for daily life, and a 12-month then/now chart. The song can be saved.

FOR RESEARCHERS

A Data detail panel shows the full 1981–2025 yearly record with a Sen's-slope trend line, Mann–Kendall significance, R², signal-to-noise (change ÷ year-to-year variability), record years, day-time vs night-time temperature change (T2M_MAX / T2M_MIN), humidity, wet-month counts, a monthly table, exact coordinates, the raw NASA query link, CSV download of every value, and a ready-made citation. Example: Kampala warms +0.28 °C per decade (p < 0.001); in Nairobi nights warmed about four times faster than days.

EIC FRAMES AS SOUND

The EIC frame view sweeps a playhead across a NASA Earth visual frame and sonifies it in real time: brightness → pitch, colour → instrument, latitude band → voice, position → stereo. It ships with NASA GIBS frames (VIIRS Black Marble night lights, MODIS true colour, GHRSST sea temperature, MODIS NDVI, MODIS land temperature) for any country or the whole Earth, and accepts any image from NASA's Earth Information Center gallery (the file stays in the browser).

WHY IT MATTERS

It makes climate change personal and local (built in Dar es Salaam for East African towns, works everywhere) and accessible to people who cannot see the maps: sound, spoken narration, keyboard control and a screen-reader live region. It is honest: it compares multi-year averages, reports whether a trend is statistically significant and explains caveats (e.g. very wet recent years such as the 2023–24 El Niño rains).

HOW WE BUILT IT

A static web app (HTML, CSS, JavaScript ES modules) with no server: Web Audio API for live synthesis (additive piano, FM electric piano, chord pad, convolution reverb), Web Speech API for narration, Leaflet for the map, NASA POWER and NASA GIBS called directly from the browser, Natural Earth for places, and Meta's open-source Astryx design-system tokens for the interface. Hosted on Netlify.

NEXT STEPS

Swahili narration, offline mode for schools, more variables (soil moisture, air quality), and a classroom "listening lab".
